CHAPTER 2 – HOME
I will discuss in this chapter how food practices and strategies contribute
to and shape Hong Kong Chinese migrants’ home-making in London, both in
terms of the domestic home and the city that they call home. The concept of
authenticity in food and cooking practices that are largely in the privacy of one’s
own home will provide a different perspective on this concept that up till this
point has been defined as an external quality, one that is pursued for show and
social advancement. I will also consider what the role of cosmopolitanism is in
relation to home; it is not only that the nature of cosmopolitanism changes when
home is in a different place, but whether in fact cosmopolitanism has become an
intrinsic part of ‘home’.
When thinking of food and home, traditional festivities as well as
everyday meals come to mind. During the period of fieldwork, there were no
traditional holidays on the Chinese calendar so I did not get a chance to formally
observe the makings of any festivities by Hong Kong migrants in London. I do
however, remember one Chinese New Year several years ago when I hosted a
potluck new year’s eve dinner (團年飯/ tyun nin faan) for a number of Chinese
friends and acquaintances. Many of the dishes people brought were very typical
for a Chinese New Year meal, but some were not; some were traditional but new,
as I had never had them with my family before. And while the setting was
completely different: friends rather than extended family and almost everyone
between the ages of twenty and thirty; the atmosphere nonetheless felt familiar
as there were elements of shared culture and tradition.
39
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
During fieldwork, when cooking and dining together with my research
participants, there was a similar sense of shared-ness and familiarity although
we had never cooked together before, and had probably learned from very
different sources. This is especially the case in Hong Kong, where many families
would have traditions that originate from their hometowns, rather than Hong
Kong itself. Therefore it would seem to be that it is not really the tangible foods,
recipes and rituals that create a home, but more importantly the intangible
shared culture and collective memory, some of which will be illustrated in the
empirical data discussed in this chapter.
In both cases of festival and everyday ritual, the sources and nature of
practices are diverse, however it is less important to discover materially what
the traditions are, than to attempt to gain an understanding of the nature of
home that is created, the processes that enable this, and how home relates to the
city in which it is situated.
In ‘Intersemiotic fruit: mangoes, multiculture and the city’, Alex Rhys-
Taylor (2014, p. 44) demonstrates how ‘global food in London is at once central
to forging affection for the city’s locales and to maintaining connections to
elsewhere’. Foods such as mangoes form a link between migrants’ homes, which
it reminds them of, and London, who’s colonial and multicultural nature are
made up of historically imported foods and smells. Even if the food is like, yet
unlike that of home, such as for Marcia: the mangoes are less fibrous that what
she remembers having as a child, they still form an important link with her
native home as well as London as her new home.
Rhys-Taylor quotes Vannini on how the sensations, particularly smells
and tastes, form a very important part of a city’s character (ibid., p.47), bringing
40
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
to mind Vannini, Waskul and Gottschalk’s (2012, p. 101) very lively description
of eating falafel in Israel, from the temperature of the food, the texture of the
sauces, the posture adopted to be able to eat without dripping on yourself to the
conversations spontaneously held. For the individual, particularly in the case of
the migrant, it is clear that the multi sensory impact of food is an important
element of cultural reproduction.
Migrant belonging is not simply a case of reproduction, but rather the
result of a process of mixed embeddedness, a concept that is adaptable from
Kloosterman and Rath’s (2001) study of migrant entrepreneurship. The authors
say that the viability of migrant entrepreneurial activity will depend not only on
the resources and networks from their past and home, but also on market
conditions and adaptations made to the new market. In a similar way, the
strengths of the practices and rituals a new migrant builds, and consequently the
quality of life in the new location will not only depend on knowledge and
resources brought from home, but also uses and reworkings of materials and
habits that may be unfamiliar but more readily available.
In this chapter I will consider the questions: what are the characteristics
of the home and home community that are created? What are the processes and
practices that go into creating home? And what does this mean for migrant
integration and belonging in society?
‘If someone came into our kitchen, would they know that it is a Chinese kitchen?’
I arrived at Claire and Wilson’s flat while Claire was preparing dinner. Her
kitchen is very compact, and we had to have the door closed in order to be able
to access the refrigerator, creating quite a cosy environment. She said that
41
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
funnily enough, she and Wilson had been discussing just a few days earlier if
their kitchen would be recognisable as a Chinese kitchen to a stranger. In Hong
Kong, kitchens are quite typically western style, but generally have no
dishwasher and no oven due to a lack to space; therefore kitchens in London
could take on a different cultural identity with a few key utensils and food items.
I had once commented that I had run out of rice and soy sauce at home and my
colleague joked that I was no longer Chinese.
(Claire’s kitchen, 26/8/14 -- photo by Claire)
42
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
(some sauces in Claire’s kitchen, 30/5/14)
While a kitchen may no longer be the heart of a household, it is the one
room in a house or flat where qualities of Chinese-ness are most visible and also
most traditional.
Claire took me through her thought process on the issue, saying that
sauces such as soy sauce and fish sauce would be commonly found in Western
kitchens given the popularity of Asian-style recipes, but things like a clay pot of
冬菜 (dung coi), a type of preserved vegetable, or oyster sauce are less
commonplace. However, she also had a collection of spirit bottles which gave the
kitchen a very fashionable feel; as well as an array of spices, which are not typical
of Cantonese seasonings. With regard to cooking utensils, she didn’t have a wok
and her rice cooker is from Argos.
Elise, on the other hand, has what I would call a very Chinese kitchen. She
has cupboards full of Chinese cooking sauces, wines, seasonings and dried
ingredients, as well as a large drawer full of instant and other types of noodles,
which are much beloved in Hong Kong for a quick and convenient meal. I also
noticed packets of Swanson chicken stock in her cupboards, a staple Hong Kong
brand, which she said her friend had brought specially for her when travelling to
the UK. Her rice cooker is a multi-use electric cooker with a rice setting; and
while she has a wok, she says she rarely uses it as it takes up too much space on
the hob.

It would seem that Hong Kong migrants, coming from a modern big city
themselves, are not too firmly wedded to tradition. For example, many favour
lighter utensils over using woks and heavy clay pots, which are traditionally
considered to give food better flavour in the name of practical considerations
such as space and ease of use. Where there is more concern with detail are the
seasonings and ingredients, which are more directly consumable, so there is
understandably a greater willingness to invest. In fact, as a few of my
participants have told me and I have the same experience, it just takes the right
sauce and seasoning to turn very ordinary ingredients from Tesco or Sainsbury’s
into an excellent Chinese dish.
During my research, I had the opportunity to cook with three groups of
participants: I visited the homes of two couples, and on the third occasion invited
one of the couples and some friends for a pot luck; as expected, the cooking
activities were mostly carried out by the women of the group. Our conversations
during cooking were quite factual, regarding the appreciation of sauces,
ingredients and sharing techniques and recipes, during eating meals as well, a
part of at least initial conversations would be devoted to appreciating tastes,
smells and textures of the food; it almost feels like a process of affirmation of
culture and identity.
In the chapter, ‘A sense of place, a sense of time’, (Vannini et al 2012,
p.112), the importance of the processes of food preparation as well as
consumption in reproducing social relations is discussed; this is because these
actions produce bonding effects and allow for ‘embodied cultural transmissions’.
It is the sharing of sensual stimuli, often equally familiar to all members of a
group, which produces the feeling of community that I have observed in my
45
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
fieldwork. What often look like repetitive or meaningless statements regarding
the food and its taste are ‘the bonding functions of vocalizing gustatory pleasures
when eating in the company of others’, as the authors quote Wiggin’s (2002)
study. Wiggins also says that eating is inherently social, and regards pleasure as
a social phenomenon inseparable from interaction and communication (ibid.,
312), and I would say that perhaps gustatory pleasure is even intensified by
interpersonal sharing.
Many words and phrases have come up during fieldwork that describe the
taste and particularly the texture of food that are quite unique to Cantonese: 滑
(waat), describing the smooth texture of meat, often in steamed dishes; and 好入
味 （hou jap mei), meaning that the flavor has really entered the food; are two
examples that come to mind. While Wiggins (ibid.) writes about the bonding
effects of the non-verbal gustatory ‘mmm’, I would speculate that words unique
to a language and cuisine would have similar or perhaps even more profound
effects.
Cooking so far would appear to be a somewhat solitary practice amongst
Hong Kong Chinese, since group food preparation activities such as making
Kimchi for the Koreans and dumplings for Northern Chinese are not something I
have found to be prevalent. However it is difficult to think of an event which
encapsulates the bonding effects of food preparation and consumption as well as
hotpot, a favourite gathering meal for Hong Kong Chinese. During hotpot, raw
ingredients and a boiling pot of soup are placed on the table and diners cook in
the communal pot and eat simultaneously. Similarly, Hong Kong style barbecues
involve each person cooking with their own barbecue fork, all sitting around the
46
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
fire. The popularity of these eating activities could well be because of the
bonding effects of not just eating but cooking together.
Most of my participants did not begin cooking for themselves regularly
until they began living in London. This could be due to a variety of factors in
Hong Kong, the main ones being living with parents or domestic helpers who do
the cooking, small kitchens and the low cost of eating out, as discussed in more
detail in the previous chapter. Some may say that cooking in London is born out
of necessity, however the pleasure many of my participants seem to derive from
this activity and the importance placed on it would suggest it is not solely the
case.
Yan talks about the basics of cooking as a student in the UK: ‘The first
thing students coming to the UK make is stir fried lettuce … and tomato fried egg,
and then they all post pictures on Facebook.’
Both of these dishes are very basic, quite homely dishes that probably
could not be found from restaurants or takeaways, which maybe another reason
to cook at home. They are also made from cheap and easy-to-handle ingredients
that are common in UK supermarkets. Yan had made stir fried lettuce with
fermented tofu at the potluck dinner, explaining that she felt that cooked lettuce
was representative of Hong Kong cooking since the vegetable was made popular
during colonial rule, and because most other cuisines only use it raw.
In both cases of cooking lettuce and tomatoes, the preparation changes
the texture of the foods quite significantly compared to if these ingredients were
used in a salad. It is a very clear illustration of how the sensory experience of
preparing, the heat of the wok and the smell etc., as well as eating differs greatly
from that, for example, of a garden salad.
47
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
So far in this chapter, it would seem that cooking sauces and flavouring
ingredients are seen as quite important in Hong Kong Chinese migrants’ kitchens
in creating satisfyingly authentic dishes; however similar practices of adjustment
and compromise in aspects of preparation as discussed in the previous chapter
are present in the cosmopolitan home. And while the embodied experience of
cooking is mostly a solitary one, one’s can always share experiences on social
media. Next we will consider the experience of sharing a meal, and the various
practices that create homeliness.
碟頭飯
vs.
食餸
/ How do you eat your meal?
At Claire and Wilson’s there was a discussion once the cooking was
finished about what utensils to use. It seemed to be a routine question for them,
as Claire poked fun at Wilson for not knowing how to use chopsticks properly.
Because they had me as a guest, Claire decided to bring the food out to the dining
area and to use bowls for rice; though she used the cooking pots to serve to
minimise washing up. She said if we were using bowls we should use chopsticks,
but Wilson insisted on a fork and spoon. They explained that generally if it were
just the two of them, they would have each person’s rice, meat and veg on a plate
each, for the convenience.
Having individual plates and each person’s own rice, meat and vegetables
on the plate is known as 碟頭飯 (dip tou faan), and is generally for a quick and
casual, and cheaper if eating out, meal. For ‘proper’ meals each person would
have their own bowl or rice and there would be several dishes of meat and
vegetables (餸/ sung) to share.
48
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
I found this habit of Claire and Wilson’s to be quite surprising, as in my
experience even casual meals at home would involve shared dishes. Using
individual plates felt alien as well as alienating, perhaps only deployed if one
person in the household was ill or on a special diet. I asked subsequent
interviewees and they had similar responses. Elise said she would not serve
individuals plates unless the meal was something non-Chinese, such as pasta or
Oyakodon.
It surprised me how personal my response felt to this unexpected
revelation by Claire. The uniformity of responses from other participants also
shows the central role food sharing has in the experience of eating a Chinese,
particularly Cantonese meal. An extreme example of a sharing dish, 盆菜 (pun
coi), literally ‘basin-food’, is a large metal container filled with various meats and
seafood heated up all together, traditionally served at large gatherings and
celebrations. In the aftermath of SARS, I felt that the more widespread use of
separate serving spoons and chopsticks also subtly changed the experience of a
meal.
Ernest brought up another interesting embodied practice when talking
about the differences when eating with non-Chinese friends. He said ‘gwailo
don’t know how to “chew bones”. The Chinese way of eating is to pick up the
piece of food and put in your rice bowl, take a bite and leave the remainder
temporarily in your own bowl. Being allowed to gnaw a piece of meat then drop
it back into the bowl is especially useful for getting the meat off bony pieces,
which is what Ernest was referring to. Because of the use of knives and forks,
Westerners are used to having food brought to their mouths only in bite size
pieces, gnawing and spitting out are not acceptable practices but are part of the
49
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
sensational landscape of eating certain Chinese foods. This brings to mind Law’s
(2001) experience of eating with her hands with Filipino workers in Hong Kong;
a Hong Kong Chinese example might be eating a chicken wing cleanly with only
chopsticks and one’s teeth.
Let us shift our attention momentarily back to the contents of a meal.
Robert observed that if he is eating Western food, a larger quantity of food is
required to achieve a feeling of fullness and satisfaction compared to if he were
eating Chinese food. This echoes the findings in Golden Arches East (Watson,
1997), in which McDonald’s customers in Beijing said they did not feel full after
eating at the fast food restaurant, since they perceived burgers to be snacks
rather than a main meal. Consuming Geographies (Bell and Valentine, 2001, p.
179) also quotes a fascinating study on rice and the Japanese, reporting similar
feelings of non-fulfilment unless rice was eaten at a meal.
Whether it is the contents or method of serving and eating a meal, it is
clear from the examples above that these practices have both emotional and
embodied impact. In the previous chapter, the authenticity regarding many
aspects of Chinese food seemed to be able to be suspended or modified without
affecting the ‘core’ of the cuisine, however in this chapter the examples appear to
have shown that these interactional aspects of ‘home’ appear to be more fragile
and less elastic than expressive characteristics of ‘identity’. In the next section, I
will look at a part of London as ‘home’ that is inevitably changing.

What language in Chinatown?
Recently in Chinatown, I can never be sure whether to address people in
shops or restaurants in Cantonese or Mandarin; in fact Holly said she would
simply speak Mandarin so as to avoid not being understood. The increasing
numbers and popularity of restaurants serving Chinese cuisine from the
Northern provinces is also evidence that not only are there increasing numbers
of Chinese migrants in London, the migrant population is also no longer majority
Cantonese (Ming-Ai, 2011).
In Chinatown itself, it can also be observed that restaurants have now
diversified from the mainly Cantonese offerings of dim sum and 燒味 (siu mei/
roasted meat) to include Northern Chinese spicy noodle shops, stalls offering
snacks to have on the go and bubble tea, which originated in Taiwan, but is also
hugely popular in Hong Kong and China.
Kitty has suggested that her taste for Chinese food has evolved and
broadened to include foods that her family would never normally eat in Hong
Kong. Therefore, she said, her taste and preference for Chinese food is through
combining old tastes with new ones, she has come to identify a broader spectrum
of food as ‘home foods’. I have also observed that when going out to dine as
group, Northern Chinese as well as other familiar Asian cuisines, such as
Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese are acceptable choices for gatherings over a
familiar or homely meal.
This shows that aside from the Internet, Chinatown and Chinese networks
in London provide Hong Kong Chinese migrants with an opportunity to get to
know Chinese foods from other regions and provinces. And it maybe the case in
London that being far away from home lets us feel closer to other ‘close to home’
51
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
foods, particularly cuisines from other Chinese provinces; which in Hong Kong
actually might be considered quite foreign.
Ernest has also shared rumours that there is criticism that Mainland
Chinese migrants working in the established, mainly Cantonese restaurants and
takeaways do not know how to cook and work in the kitchens; and even that new
takeaways operated by Mainland migrants use substandard ingredients.
While discussing the changes in Chinatown, particularly the language
ambiguity, I have not observed any particularly negative emotions of sadness or
missing the way things were; Ernest’s comments are unsubstantiated but show
the ambivalent attitude many Hong Kong Chinese have towards Mainlanders
nowadays, given increasing tensions between Hong Kong people and Mainland
visitors and new residents in Hong Kong (BBC, 2012).
When considering the relationship between migrants in my target group,
Chinatown and London, it is important to remember that the background of my
participants would have very little in common with ‘natives’ of Chinatown, who
would mostly either have family in London who have lived here for several
generations, or are new migrants with relatively limited language and
employment skills, or work in industries that almost solely serve Chinese
customers. For migrants that are the subject of this dissertation, Chinatown
would be a relatively small part of their lives, visited perhaps as infrequently as
once every few months.
‘The pigeon and the weave’ (Jackson, 2014) demonstrates the delicacy of
the balance of multiculturalism, using the example of Rye Lane in Peckham,
where it is difficult to achieve a desirable mix which does not arouse feelings of
disgust and unease, but has not become too tame and gentrified. It also shows
52
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
how changes in the multicultural composition of an area or indeed a city can
occur without one noticing, but once it happens alters the character of the place
irreversibly. The substantial changes in Chinatown reflect a growing Mainland
Chinese population in London, slowly becoming apparent through more snatches
of Mandarin heard on the street, and suddenly observing that I would be
addressed by ‘ni hao’ instead of ‘konichiwa’ by random strangers.
While the changing face of Chinatown and more broadly the Chinese
population in London has not apparently had a large impact on the Hong Kong
Chinese migrant’s experience of London as a hometown; I feel that there are
greater changes, both in scale and impact, yet to come as China is becoming more
prominent in the global political, economic and social landscape, and the number
of Chinese abroad, both as tourists and migrants increase.
